Collins analyzes bipedal as bi- plus pedal adjective, with foot meaning; the frozen source explicitly marks -pedal as a suffix and the form is word-final. Accept as source-scoped foot-family lookup suffix. Preserve prior competing biped + -al analysis as history.

Dictionary.com identifies centipedal as a centipede derivative; AHD gives centipeda from centi- plus Latin pes/ped- foot. Wiktionary explicitly lists centipedal under -pedal and calls its segmentation a surface analysis. The frozen source also lists -pedal as a suffix. Accept as word-final foot-family lookup variant for centipede-related senses; preserve competing derivational analysis.

Webster 1913 analyzes decempedal as Latin decem plus English pedal; 1828 Webster gives Latin pes foot. Frozen source explicitly marks -pedal as a suffix, and this word ends with the form. Accept as a source-scoped foot-family lookup suffix, retaining historical competing analyses.

Century analyzes quadrupedal as quadruped + -al, and quadruped ultimately contains Latin ped- foot. The source lists -pedal as a suffix; this foot-family form is word-final, and extends across no other root. Accept as a family lookup variant for four-footed sense, without claiming it is the sole modern segmentation.

Webster defines semipedal as half a foot in length. Century traces its base semiped to Latin semipes, semi- plus pes/ped- foot. Frozen source lists -pedal as a suffix; the word-final foot-family form supports a lookup variant for the measurement sense. A distinct metrical half-foot sense is documented and is not asserted to mean a measured length.

Collins gives Latin sesquipedalis from sesqui- plus pedalis of the foot; AHD confirms pes/ped- foot. Source identifies -pedal as suffix and the word ends in it. Accept as a word-final historical-family lookup variant, without claiming a unique modern segmentation.
